title: Community Nutrition Institute v. Young (1987)
summary: FDA action levels for food contaminants were legislative rules requiring notice and comment because the agency's own regulations and statements gave them present binding effect, while its refusal to prosecute blended corn was unreviewable enforcement discretion.
notes:
Key line: "For here, we are convinced that FDA has bound itself." (per curiam)

Citation: 818 F.2d 943 (D.C. Cir. 1987).

sections.Parties: The appellants were the Community Nutrition Institute, a consortium of consumer organizations, and Laura A. Rogers, a private citizen, referred to collectively as CNI. The appellee was Frank Young, Commissioner of the Food and Drug Administration. The State of South Carolina, whose corn growers had been permitted to blend contaminated corn, filed an amicus brief supporting FDA. The case was before the United States Court of Appeals for the District of Columbia Circuit for the second time, on remand from the Supreme Court, and was decided by a panel of Judges Mikva, Edwards and Starr.
sections.Material Facts: Aflatoxins are by products of molds that grow on corn and other crops. Under 21 U.S.C. section 346, which directs FDA to limit unavoidable poisonous or deleterious substances in food, FDA set action levels telling producers how much contamination it would tolerate; the level for aflatoxin in corn was 20 parts per billion. FDA's regulations, 21 C.F.R. section 109.4, said an action level may be established to define the level of contamination at which food will be deemed to be adulterated, and section 109.8 let FDA exempt from regulatory action food that is unlawfully contaminated above an action level. In a 1981 Federal Register notice permitting blending, FDA stated that food containing aflatoxin above 20 parts per billion is considered adulterated and may not be shipped in interstate commerce. FDA had several times allowed contaminated corn to be blended with clean corn to bring the mixture within the action level. The action levels were issued without notice and comment.
sections.Procedural History: CNI sued in the United States District Court for the District of Columbia, claiming that the action level violated the rulemaking requirements of the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act, that it was a legislative rule issued without notice and comment in violation of the APA, and that permitting blending violated the Act. The district court granted summary judgment to FDA on all three claims. The court of appeals initially held that the Act required formal regulations rather than action levels, 757 F.2d 354 (1985), without reaching the other issues. The Supreme Court reversed, holding the statute ambiguous and FDA's interpretation permissible, 476 U.S. 974 (1986), and remanded. On remand the court of appeals heard argument on December 19, 1986, and on May 15, 1987, held the action levels invalid for want of notice and comment, rejected the blending claim, and remanded to the district court.
sections.Issue: Whether FDA's action levels for aflatoxin in corn fell within the exception in 5 U.S.C. section 553(b)(3)(A) for interpretative rules and general statements of policy, as FDA contended, or were legislative rules that could be issued only after notice and comment. And whether FDA's decisions to permit blending of adulterated corn with unadulterated corn violated the adulteration provisions of the Food, Drug and Cosmetic Act or were instead unreviewable exercises of enforcement discretion under Heckler v. Chaney.
sections.Holding: The court held that the action levels were legislative rules subject to notice and comment. Applying the criteria of American Bus Association v. United States, whether the pronouncement has a present binding effect and whether it leaves the agency free to exercise discretion, the court found that FDA's regulations spoke of action levels defining adulteration and prohibiting substances, that FDA required exceptions before contaminated food could be marketed, and that FDA's formal and informal statements treated food above the level as adulterated. FDA had bound itself, even though producers could still contest adulteration in an enforcement suit. The court held that the blending decisions were unreviewable because FDA has complete discretion not to bring enforcement proceedings.
sections.Reasoning: The per curiam opinion acknowledged that the line between legislative and interpretative rules is enshrouded in considerable smog, and that courts give some but not overwhelming deference to an agency's own characterization while attaching great weight to the words the agency actually used. Three factors were decisive. First, FDA's regulations described action levels as defining the level at which food will be deemed adulterated and as able to prohibit any detectable amount of a substance. Second, FDA required producers to obtain exemptions to market food above an action level, which implied that such food was otherwise unlawful, a status that could derive only from the action level itself. Third, FDA's telegram to South Carolina and its Federal Register notice declared corn above 20 parts per billion adulterated and barred from interstate commerce. The court accepted that in an enforcement suit FDA would still have to prove adulteration rather than mere noncompliance, so producers were not fully bound, but the agency had cabined its own prosecutorial discretion, and under Guardian Federal a policy statement that narrowly limits administrative discretion is a binding rule of substantive law. The holding was narrow: FDA could still use action levels as pure policy statements if it stopped giving them substantive significance. On blending, the court agreed that blended corn is adulterated but held that the complaint amounted to a demand that FDA prosecute, which Heckler v. Chaney places beyond judicial review.

topics.lrs-n-guidance: Action levels could bind FDA’s enforcement policy even though the agency still had to prove statutory adulteration in court.
topics.lrs-o-section-553: The case turns on whether the action levels had to go through § 553 notice and comment or fell within the § 553(b)(A) exemptions for interpretive rules and policy statements.
topics.lrs-n-interpretive-rules: FDA defended the action levels as interpretive rules or policy statements; the court's binding-effect test is the standard exam tool for distinguishing them from legislative rules.

learning.separateOpinions: Judge Starr concurred in Part II, upholding FDA's enforcement discretion over blending, and dissented from Part I. He argued that the court should return to the single factor test of Pacific Gas & Electric Co. v. FPC: a pronouncement is a legislative rule only if it has the force of law in subsequent proceedings, so that the agency need only show the rule was violated. Because FDA in any enforcement action must prove that corn is actually adulterated and cannot merely show noncompliance with the action level, the action level had no force of law at all and was a policy statement, although he conceded that the majority's approach was faithful to recent circuit precedent and buttressed by common sense.
